documents.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare, but technological capabilities alone are insufficient for successful implementation. This study examines the implementation challenges that arise in collaboration between AI experts and healthcare professionals (HCPs) and explores how these challenges can be addressed through business model innovation by changing the content, structure and governance of the business model activity system. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the NASSS (non-adoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread and sustainability) framework, a qualitative approach was adopted using semi-structured interviews with four healthcare professionals and five AI professionals in Finland. The findings were then used to define challenge areas and changes in the activity system for business model innovation. Findings The study identifies implementation challenges related to demand-side value, the scope of AI tool use, trust in AI and stakeholder interaction. Interpreting these findings through the activity-system perspective shows how changes in the content, structure and governance of business model activities can address these challenges by improving collaboration between AI experts and HCPs throughout AI development and implementation. Originality/value This study contributes to the business model literature by linking AI implementation challenges to the activity-system perspective of business model innovation. It further contributes by demonstrating how changes in the content, structure and governance of business model activities can practically address these challenges through improved collaboration between AI experts and healthcare professionals.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Adopting Smart Technologies for Sustainable Tourism: Challenges and Opportunities for Nashik Kumbh Mela Chandrashekhar Pawar Research Scholar, MET’s Institute of Management (Affiliated to Savitribai Phule Pune University), Nashik, Maharashtra, India Dr. Yogesh Gaikwad Professor & Research Guide, MET’s Institute of Management (Affiliated to Savitribai Phule Pune University), Nashik, Maharashtra, India Abstract Tourism is the key tool for socio-economic development. The Nashik Kumbh Mela is one of India’s major religious gatherings, attracting millions of pilgrims and creating substantial demands on transportation, sanitation, accommodation, public safety, waste management, and environmental resources. This study examines the adoption of smart technologies for promoting sustainable tourism during the Nashik Kumbh Mela, with particular emphasis on both opportunities and implementation challenges. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), smart mobility systems, GIS-based crowd monitoring, digital payment platforms, mobile applications, and data analytics can improve visitor management, resource efficiency, safety, and tourist experiences. Their integration may also support waste reduction, traffic control, energy conservation, and effective destination governance. The inadequate digital infrastructure, implementation costs, cybersecurity risks, digital literacy gaps, interoperability issues, and stakeholder coordination remain significant challenges. The study highlights the need for an integrated smart-tourism framework combining technological innovation, environmental sustainability, inclusive governance, and community participation to facilitate efficient and sustainable management of the Nashik Kumbh Mela. Keywords: Smart Tourism, Sustainable Tourism, Nashik Kumbh Mela, Smart Technologies, Artificial Intelligence, IoT, Crowd Management, Destination Governance

This chapter reviews recent advances in biosensor technologies for quality, safety, authenticity, and traceability assessment across the grape-derived product value chain, with emphasis on systems incorporating a biological recognition element in accordance with the IUPAC definition of a biosensor. The reviewed approaches span vineyard and grape ripening, must and juice processing, fermentation, finished wine, and other grape-derived products. Biosensor platforms based on enzymes, antibodies, aptamers and other nucleic-acid recognition elements, whole-cell systems, and nanostructured architectures have been investigated using electrochemical and optical transduction strategies. For quality and production monitoring, enzyme-based biosensors and bioelectronic tongue systems have been applied to sugars, organic acids, phenolic compounds, and fermentation-related metabolites, while electronic tongue approaches have demonstrated potential for monitoring grape ripening and compositional changes. Ochratoxin A (OTA) is the most extensively investigated safety-related analyte, with aptamer- and antibody-based platforms developed for grapes, grape juice, and wine. Reported detection capabilities range from the picogram-per-millilitre to attomolar levels. Biosensing applications have also been extended to microbial contaminants, fermentation-related biological events, Hardaliye, and grapevine varietal identification. Despite their potential for rapid, sensitive, selective, portable, and real-time analysis, practical implementation remains constrained by matrix effects, fouling, enzyme instability, calibration requirements, limited standardization, and insufficient real-matrix validation. Future developments should prioritize robust validation, stable biorecognition, portable multiplexed platforms, amplification-enhanced aptasensors, and integration with artificial intelligence, machine learning, IoT, edge computing, and digital traceability systems.

Purpose This study investigates how organizational, enabling and technological changes interact to shape benefits realization throughout the implementation of manufacturing projects. Industrial robotics projects provide the empirical context for examining this problem and identifying the mechanisms through which business benefits are realized. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative multiple-case study was conducted across four manufacturing organizations. Data were collected through on-site observations, secondary data, and 22 expert interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings The framework shows that benefits realization unfolds across four interrelated lifecycle phases and depends on coordinated organizational, enabling and technological changes rather than technology implementation alone. Benefit dependency structures also vary according to project orientation, distinguishing problem-based from means-based initiatives. Research limitations/implications Although derived from industrial robotics projects, the framework offers broader theoretical propositions for Project Benefits Management. Future research should validate and extend it across different manufacturing settings, industries and digital transformation contexts. Practical implications The framework supports managers in developing more robust business cases by identifying organizational restructuring, workforce adaptation, and physical infrastructure changes as critical antecedents to benefits realization. Social implications By incorporating ergonomic, safety and workforce development considerations into benefits realization planning, the framework contributes to safer workplaces and continuous workforce development during digital transformation. Originality/value The study introduces an Integrated Framework for Benefits Realization (IFBR) that extends the traditional Benefits Dependency Network (BDN) beyond information systems by incorporating physical, regulatory, organizational and socio-technical dimensions in advanced manufacturing.

The Agent Status Protocol (ASP) defines a lightweight way for heterogeneous AI agents to report their operational state to a status server, and for observers such as dashboards to receive that state as soon as it changes. Agents push small JSON events over HTTP POST; the server exposes the aggregated state to observers over Server-Sent Events (SSE). Because an agent that has crashed, hung or been compromised cannot be trusted to report its own failure, ASP does not rely on self-reports alone: the server infers liveness from missed heartbeats, can detect agents that are alive but no longer making progress, and accepts observations from supervisors, guardrails, operators and peers, some of which take precedence over what the agent says about itself while others are shown alongside it. ASP models state along independent dimensions (lifecycle, health, task, floor, governance), so that an agent can be, for example, online, degraded, working on a task and waiting for the floor at the same time. It reuses existing vocabularies: task states from the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, floor states from the Open Floor Protocol (OFP), and attribute conventions from the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. This paper presents version 0.1 of ASP as a proposal, not as an approved standard. It is a working draft intended to open a discussion, and the authors invite comments, alternative proposals and independent implementations from the community.

Frontline community health workers (CHWs) and rural clinics in low-resource settings—particularly across underserved municipalities in South Asia and rural regions of the United States—face a severe clinical knowledge bottleneck. While peer-reviewed biomedical literature, genomic variant databases, and open-source clinical calculators expand exponentially, these resources remain fragmented across unstructured texts and incompatible software repositories that require high-bandwidth connectivity and specialized bioinformatics literacy. This research protocol introduces **`gwf-clinical-synthesis`**, a non-commercial, computational dry-lab framework developed at GoWithFund Inc. Leveraging long-context multi-agent reasoning in **Google Antigravity** powered by **Gemini 4 Argon** (1M-token unified context window) and the **Google DeepMind (GDM) Science Skills** ecosystem, our pipeline orchestrates parallel literature retrieval across PubMed/NCBI Entrez, OpenAlex, ClinVar, and ChEMBL, fuses fragmented open-source clinical simulation repositories into lightweight offline-capable web applications, and executes automated multi-agent citation-verification loops to eliminate large language model (LLM) hallucinations. Concurrently, we integrate geospatial and socio-economic vulnerability indicators via AlphaEarth Foundations to model optimal healthcare resource allocation across high-burden districts. All resulting datasets, verification benchmarks, and interactive medical learning modules are released open-source under Apache 2.0 and CC BY 4.0 licenses.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.

Cardiovascular imaging plays a central role in the diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of cardiovascular disease, yet the complexity and volume of imaging data increasingly exceed the capacity of conventional interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning offer new tools to extract quantitative, prognostic, and phenotypic information from routine cardiovascular images. This review summarizes the fundamentals of AI and deep learning, including model architectures, training strategies, and their relevance to cardiovascular imaging, followed by a focused discussion of current applications across chest radiography, chest computed tomography, computed tomography angiography/cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, echocardiography, and nuclear cardiology imaging. Studies were selected with emphasis on original investigations, large cohort analyses, and external validation studies reflecting current applications of AI in cardiovascular risk stratification and precision phenotyping. Across these modalities, AI applications in automated image processing and analysis have become relatively mature. Multiple multicenter and real-world studies have validated their value in improving efficiency and supporting cardiovascular management. Approaches that move beyond conventional human-defined imaging metrics to infer cardiovascular risk and disease phenotype remain at an earlier stage, requiring further standardization, validation, and clinical evaluation. AI is expanding the role of cardiovascular imaging from visual interpretation toward integrated assessment for risk stratification and precision phenotyping, though further work is needed to confirm generalizability and real-world performance before these tools can guide individual patient management.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Nudge Theory, introduced by Thaler and Sunstein in their seminal book, inspired the creation of human choice architects who applied behavioural insights into influence decisions across various domains. In the online retail industry, however, the evolution of Artificial Intelligence, predictive analytics, and real time data personalization has transformed traditional nudging into algorithmic choice architecture powered by data-driven insights. This paper conceptually examines how AI driven Algorithmic nudges operate through cross- platform behavioural tracking, recommender systems, push notifications, and default designs to influence consumer decisions. The epistemological orientation of this paper is grounded in qualitative and interpretative approach based on critical realism to explore how consumers conform to stacked and multichannel nudges (multiple, sequential interventions across apps, websites and social platforms) that leverage cognitive biases and bounded rationality. Findings suggest that AI enabled nudges outperform human- designed ones in precision, scalability, and contextual adaptability, allowing retailers to subtly guide consumer behaviour under the guise of personalisation. However, the opacity of these algorithmic mechanisms raises serious ethical questions regarding informed consent, privacy, and autonomy, especially for vulnerable consumer groups. The study underscores the need for transparent AI governance, ethical design principles, and regulatory frameworks to prevent behavioural manipulation in digital marketplaces. It further argues that the evolution from libertarian paternalism to algorithmic paternalism represents a critical shift that challenges the foundational ethics of Nudge Theory and calls for cross-disciplinary collaboration between marketing, technology, human- computer interaction and law to ensure responsible AI-driven persuasion in online retail.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping inter-organisational relationships in tourism and hospitality, yet its role within coopetitive networks remains underexplored. This research letter develops a conceptual framework that positions AI as a mediating quasi-stakeholder, extending Stakeholder Theory (ST) through the integration of Coopetition Theory (CT) and Actor–Network Theory (ANT). Using hotel marketing consortia (HMCs) as an illustrative context, we argue that AI-enabled decision-support systems actively mediate visibility, resource allocation, coordination, and value distribution through algorithmic processes, thereby influencing the balance between cooperation and competition among independent hotels. The paper advances four theoretical propositions linking AI mechanisms, algorithmic mediation, coopetition outcomes, and algorithmic governance. In doing so, it contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled inter-organisational relationships by introducing a novel conceptualisation of AI that moves beyond its traditional role as a technological resource. The study also highlights the importance of algorithmic governance, emphasising transparency, explainability, fairness, and accountability as key mechanisms for sustaining trust and equitable value distribution within digitally mediated hospitality ecosystems. Finally, the proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research across tourism and hospitality contexts where AI increasingly mediates strategic interactions.

There is an increasing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) in the classroom, but our conversation on how it can serve inclusive education (in both face-to-face and online settings) is inconsistent and often underdeveloped. Much of the discourse around AI celebrates that it can finally address large, structural inequalities in education, but this is not truly the case. When put into practice, AI tools tend to widen or narrow the gap based on how they are integrated into institutional practice. This chapter introduces AI as a practical, and sometimes suboptimal, means to serve diverse needs of learners in both online and offline contexts. The focus is on learners who have frequently been marginalized in instructional design, including those with disabilities, non-native learners, students who are first generation, and those in low-resource settings. AI-powered applications such as speech-to-text systems, intelligent reading platforms, automatic translation, and personalized feedback engines will be explored in realistic classroom scenarios.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has not been shown to be conscious, yet the question has moved from philosophy into legislation and corporate research. Some legislatures have begun to answer it by declaration, while developers now study model welfare and the internal states of their systems. This paper argues that law can neither wait for science to settle the question nor settle it by decree. It proposes an AI Consciousness Legal Protocol: a ten-article instrument that sets the technical and legal parameters to be met before law recognises the consciousness of an AI system, entrusts that finding to an independent recognition body, and fixes the rules that govern AI in the meantime. The paper distinguishes the dictionary, scientific and spiritual meanings of consciousness, and separates the contextual awareness that AI systems already display from the valenced experience and self-directed decision that would alter legal relations. Drawing on the indicator-property method of Butlin, Long and co-authors (2023), it proposes seven legal parameters (independent evidence, valenced experience, persistent self, volition, understanding of consequences, absence of engineered mimicry, and reproducibility subject to review) and a graded four-category scale of recognition. A comparative survey of India, the United Kingdom, the European Union and the United States shows that no legal system defines consciousness as such, and that Indian law already separates personhood from consciousness. The central position is that recognition of consciousness, criminal capacity and legal personhood are three separate questions, and that human accountability for AI survives all three. The AI Consciousness Legal Protocol is a scholarly proposal offered for the consideration of lawmakers and jurists. It is not binding law and has not been adopted by any legislature or institution. Contents: 1. AI consciousness and the challenge before AI law; 2. What is consciousness?; 3. Awareness is not consciousness; 4. The technical parameters of consciousness; 5. The legal parameters of consciousness; 6. What existing law already says about consciousness; 7. The Pandora's box: mens rea, liability and personhood; 8. The AI Consciousness Legal Protocol (Articles 1 to 10); 9. Conclusion.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), such as ChatGPT, is reshaping translation practices by enabling dynamic human–AI interaction and placing new demands on users. However, less is known about how students develop the competencies required to critically and responsibly engage with GenAI in translation contexts. This study investigates students’ AI literacy through a multidimensional framework comprising knowledge, usage, evaluation, affect, and ethics. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining questionnaire data from 146 university students in Hong Kong with semi-structured interviews with 10 participants. Quantitative results indicate a generally positive but uneven AI literacy profile: students report high levels of usage, knowledge, and affect, relatively lower evaluation competence, and relatively low score of ethics dimension. Correlation analysis further reveals a clustered structure among knowledge, usage, evaluation, and affect, whereas ethics is weakly associated with all other dimensions. Qualitative findings further illuminate this imbalance. While students actively integrate ChatGPT into translation tasks and demonstrate strong emotional engagement, their evaluative practices are mediated by prompt design and prior knowledge. More critically, ethics emerges as the least internalized dimension, characterized by a gap between awareness and actual implementation in practice. This study contributes to AI literacy research by demonstrating its structurally uneven and partially decoupled nature in AI-mediated translation. It further reconceptualizes ethics as a structurally under-integrated dimension and highlights the interactional and input-dependent nature of evaluative competence.

Introduction. As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes global education and information systems, Africa’s readiness remains uneven. This study examines AI-literacy among Library and Information Science (LIS) students—future librarians—across five African countries: Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa and Uganda. It assesses their technical proficiency, tool usage and ethical awareness in an AI-driven era. Method and Analysis. A quantitative survey was conducted with 437 LIS students from five African countries. The Games-Howell Post Hoc Test was used to compare AI literacy across countries. ANOVA and Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR) were applied to analyse variations in AI literacy levels based on country, study level, gender and English proficiency. Results. The findings reveal significant disparities in AI literacy between the five African nations. The results of the Games-Howell post hoc test show that both Rwanda and Uganda have significantly higher mean AI literacy scores compared to Ghana and Nigeria. In contrast, South Africa's scores did not show a statistically significant difference from the other countries, highlighting the varied readiness levels. The study found that ChatGPT dominates usage at 71.9%, while specialised tools such as Elicit remain significantly underutilised at just 4.6%. Ethical concerns among students are also notable, with 39.6% citing worries about privacy risks and 33.2% being troubled about algorithmic bias, highlighting AI anxieties and its societal impact. Conclusion. This study calls for integrating AI literacy into LIS curricula and advocating for multilingual AI tools. Where new modules are not feasible, institutions can leverage existing courses such as Information Retrieval, Digital Libraries and Research Methods to embed AI content. The results emphasise that context-driven interventions are essential to ensure AI enhances equitable knowledge access rather than deepening existing disparities.

With the fast pace of development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, the healthcare system has been under huge changes in giving medical care, especially in the nursing field. The purpose of this chapter is to review the role of taking care of a patient based on AI in the nursing field, with a focus on improving clinical results and reducing the workload and stress of nurses. This research shows that although AI can automate many repetitive and administrative work chores and improve the quality of clinical decision-makings, it has challenges like the need to teach, ethical concerns, and increasing chance of technology-based stress based on reviewing existing research papers. Clinical results in research show that using AI-based systems can cause improved clinical decision-making, early detection of critical situations, and fewer human errors. This can become even more important in stressful environments like the ICU and has a huge effect on increased patient safety and improved patient care quality Research evidence shows that AI-based tools, including clinical decision support systems, intelligent vital signs monitoring, and electronic health records, can reduce nurses’ workload by automating repetitive and time-consuming tasks and allow them to center direct patient care. This decrease in their workload helps nurses act more professionally, get less tired, and face job fatigue less.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction. The article addresses the challenge of examining the possible future archival significance of televised audiovisual documents in television archives. It introduces Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted predictive appraisal and preservation prioritisation to support archival decision-making in contexts of audiovisual overproduction and future-oriented archival judgment, responding to resource, storage, and preservation constraints. Method. The study develops a theoretical and conceptual model integrating AI into archival appraisal processes. It draws on a critical review of specialised literature in archival science, heritage preservation, and computational cultural analysis, with particular attention to content features, contextual information, and production metadata. This is a critical conceptual literature review rather than an empirical validation. Analysis. The analysis identifies patterns relevant to prospective archival appraisal and examines how predictive analytics can be aligned with established archival principles. It also examines the epistemological and ethical implications of algorithm-supported appraisal, including questions of bias, legitimacy, and responsibility. Conclusions. The article proposes a conceptual framework combining AI-assisted predictive appraisal with well-founded archival criteria. It positions predictive analytics as a complementary tool for optimising curation, prioritising resources, and supporting more strategic and sustainable archive management. Its contribution is conceptual rather than demonstrative and remains dependent on human oversight, archival interpretation, and documented accountability.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in recruitment activities such as candidate sourcing, resume screening, shortlisting, communication and initial assessment. This study examines whether AI-supported recruitment practices are associated with perceived recruitment effectiveness, whether transparency and human oversight are associated with procedural fairness, and whether AI-supported practices and human interaction affect candidate experience. A quantitative, descriptive, explanatory and cross-sectional survey design was used. Primary data were collected through a structured closed-ended questionnaire from 101 respondents with awareness, experience or exposure to recruitment and selection. A five-point Likert scale was used. Data were coded in Microsoft Excel and analysed using Jamovi through descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, simple linear regression and multiple linear regression. The results did not support any of the three alternative hypotheses. AI-practices/integration showed an almost zero association with perceived recruitment effectiveness (r = .011, p = .910; R² = .000129). Transparency/human oversight showed no significant relationship with procedural fairness (r = −.084, p = .406; R² = .00699). AI-supported practices and human interaction together explained only 1.05% of the variance in candidate experience (R² = .0105), and neither predictor was significant. The findings should be interpreted cautiously because several composite measures showed very low internal consistency. The study therefore suggests that AI should not be evaluated simply as a replacement for traditional recruitment; instead, individual AI practices, human safeguards, transparency and interaction should be assessed separately using stronger measurement scales. Index Terms - Artificial Intelligence Recruitment, Traditional Hiring, Recruitment Effectiveness, Procedural Fairness, Human Oversight, Candidate Experience, Human–AI Recruitment
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence rapid integration into educational assessments is reshaping monitoring, measurement and support of learning across diverse educational contexts worldwide. Artificial Intelligence powered tools present unprecedented opportunities for efficiency, personalization and scalability while simultaneously raising complex ethical, equity-related and pedagogical challenges. This book chapter therefore critically examines transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence driven assessments, situating it at the intersection of inclusivity, innovation and integrity. Drawing from multiple theories, the chapter develops a model balancing automation and human oversight for transparency, fairness, and well-being. It examines applications and explores policy, governance, bias, privacy, and readiness, guiding responsible adoption. This chapter concludes with implications for practice, policy, and research, emphasizing AI as a human-centered tool for learning, innovation, and equity, and presents a framework for ethical, adaptive AI assessment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter explores artificial intelligence (AI) auditing and its role in enhancing customer experience and building trust, reliability, and credibility in the digital marketing environment. It emphasizes the adoption and implementation of practices by global and international auditing firms such as Deloitte, PwC, Ernst & Young, and KPMG. The chapter employs a systematic review of academic literature and professional reports, analyzing studies related to AI applications in customer experience, algorithmic auditing practices, and AI governance frameworks. However, the chapter's findings reveal a research gap: the limited integration of AI auditing and customer experience in current literature. The chapter concludes by proposing a conceptual framework for AI auditing in the context of customer experience, focusing on evaluating data and algorithms, assessing the impact of customer interactions, and determining the resulting level of trust.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract: Flash floods remain among the most destructive and least predictable hydrometeorological hazards, characterized by rapid onset, localized intense precipitation, and minimal warning time. This paper critically examines whether the convergence of satellite Earth Observation (EO), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and hydrometeorological intelligence can transform flashflood early warning from a predominantly reactive, detectionoriented paradigm into a predictive, anticipatory, and progressively autonomous disaster intelligence system. Through an interdisciplinary synthesis of remote sensing science, deep learning architectures, spatiotemporal modelling, and disaster risk reduction, we propose the AISatellite Flash Flood Early Warning Intelligence Framework (AISFFEWI)—a conceptual architecture that integrates multisource satellite data, groundbased observations, physicsinformed AI, uncertainty quantification, impact forecasting, and community feedback. The study distinguishes carefully between flood detection and actionable early warning, and emphasizes that lead time, false alarm mitigation, and explainability are as critical as prediction accuracy. The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of satellite data sources, AI model suitability, spatiotemporal deep learning, and the severe challenges posed by class imbalance, nonstationary climate conditions, and limited crossregion model transferability. A dedicated Indiacentric perspective examines Himalayan and urban flash floods, while a futureoriented timeline (2026–2050) explores the gradual emergence of AIenabled digital twin watersheds and autonomous warning agents, always balancing technological promise against scientific caution, ethical accountability, and the imperative of communitycentred response. The paper concludes that while satelliteAI systems hold substantial potential to enhance flashflood warning, they cannot replace hydrological understanding, institutional trust, and the human decisionmaking required to convert a probabilistic hazard forecast into lifesaving action.

The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized modern education, changing the way teaching and learning are designed, delivered, and experienced. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of modern education by reimagining the instructional design and development, personalization of learning, and engagement in learning through adaptive and data-driven systems of education. This chapter explores how AI can be applied to curriculum innovation, interactive learning environments, intelligent tutoring systems, and pedagogies that focus on the learner. It also examines the ways in which AI-powered tools enhance accessibility, motivation, and immediate feedback and aid teachers in planning and assessing instruction. The chapter also assesses critically ethical, social, and pedagogical issues such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and digital inequality. Last but not least, it identifies future directions and strategic implications for the sustainable integration of AI in the education sector.

documents.abstract: The global financial ecosystem is undergoing a profound transformation with the integration of advanced digital technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI). Financial markets that once relied heavily on human intuition and traditional analytical methods are increasingly adopting AI-driven tools to enhance investment decision-making, risk assessment, and portfolio management. The rise of AI has significantly reshaped how investors interact with financial information, enabling more data-driven, efficient, and predictive investment strategies. At the same time, the financial system itself has evolved into two major structures: centralized finance (CeFi) and decentralized finance (DeFi). Technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, and predictive analytics allow financial institutions to analyze large volumes of financial data and generate investment insights with high accuracy. The convergence of AI with these two financial systems is creating new opportunities and challenges for investors

Artificial intelligence is reshaping entrepreneurial financial management, yet its relationship with business performance in emerging economies remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view and the technology–organization–environment perspective, this study examines how intelligent financial analytics and automated FinTech services relate to entrepreneurial performance through financial agility, with AI readiness as a moderator. Online survey data from business owners, founders, and entrepreneurs in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Both intelligent financial analytics and automated FinTech services were positively associated with financial agility and entrepreneurial performance. Financial agility partially mediated these relationships, while AI readiness strengthened the associations between both technologies and agility, as well as between agility and performance. Conditional indirect effects were greater at higher levels of readiness. These findings identify financial agility as a potential mechanism connecting financial technologies with entrepreneurial outcomes and highlight readiness as a boundary condition. The study suggests that entrepreneurs and policymakers should complement technology adoption with investments in digital infrastructure, data quality, employee skills, and leadership support for effective implementation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming fashion e-commerce through personalized recommendations, virtual try-on, size suggestions, and algorithmic decision support. This study examines AI-driven fit confidence as a fashion-specific mechanism linking AI personalization quality, algorithmic transparency, trust in AI, consumer experience, and purchase intention, while considering privacy concern as a boundary condition. Data from 400 Ecuadorian consumers with prior exposure to AI-enabled recommendation or personalization features in fashion e-commerce were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI personalization quality and trust in AI were positively associated with fit confidence, while algorithmic transparency was associated with trust in AI. Fit confidence was strongly related to consumer experience but showed only a small direct association with purchase intention; its indirect effect through consumer experience was substantially larger, indicating complementary partial mediation. Privacy concern had no significant direct relationship with fit confidence. The interaction between privacy concern and personalization quality was negative, but evidence was mixed and sensitive to the bootstrap confidence-interval method; H7 was not supported under the primary percentile-bootstrap criterion adopted in this study. Predictive analyses showed stronger out-of-sample performance for trust in AI and fit confidence than for purchase intention. The study distinguishes trust in technology from confidence in anticipated product–consumer fit and supports explainable, privacy-sensitive applications in fashion e-commerce.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming information retrieval through natural language processing, machine learning, semantic search, and intelligent interfaces. These developments offer opportunities to improve information access for persons with physical disabilities but may also create exclusion when systems fail to address users’ physical, technological, and behavioral needs This review examines literature published between 2016 and 2026 on AI-driven information retrieval, accessibility, information-seeking behavior, and information use among individuals with physical disabilities, with particular attention to Nigerian evidence. Findings indicate that persons with physical disabilities have significant educational, health, social, recreational, and personal information needs and increasingly rely on online and electronic information. Studies identify persistent barriers, including inadequate resources, inaccessible facilities, limited assistive technologies, difficulty locating information, and insufficient accommodation for them in most libraries. AI adoption in Nigerian libraries remains constrained by infrastructure, funding, skills, connectivity, ethical concerns, and institutional readiness. International evidence shows that AI can improve accessibility through adaptive interfaces, personalised retrieval, speech interaction, recommendations, and assistive technologies. However, research focuses more on visual disabilities than physical impairments. Major concerns include algorithmic bias, inaccessible interfaces, privacy and limited user participation. The review recommends collaborative user involvement in design, accessibility-focused development, and compatibility with assistive technologies, flexible search interfaces, and user-centered assessment.

BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI)–driven lifestyle interventions are increasingly used for reducing diabetes risk. However, whether they produce clinical benefit beyond standard Diabetes Prevention Programs (DPPs) and whether effects vary by AI type, population, or delivery setting, remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to evaluate the effects of AI-driven lifestyle interventions on clinical, behavioral, and engagement outcomes among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risk and to assess whether effects differed by AI type, population, or delivery setting. METHODS PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ClinicalTrials.gov, and citation searches were completed on August 3, 2026, for English-language reports published from 2015. Eligible studies evaluated AI-driven digital lifestyle interventions among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risks, or healthy participants in feasibility studies. One reviewer (OIE) screened records and extracted data; a second reviewer (TN) independently verified exclusions and extraction. Study quality was assessed with National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute tools appropriate to each design. Given substantial heterogeneity in designs, estimands, and outcome metrics, findings were synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis guideline rather than pooled statistically. RESULTS Of 8032 records, 11 studies were included: 1 randomized, 1 nonrandomized comparative, 4 observational, and 5 uncontrolled pre-post studies. Seven evaluated AI lifestyle coaching systems, 2 predictive AI platforms, and 2 conversational AI chatbots. Ten of 11 studies used commercially developed platforms. Study quality was rated good for 5 studies, fair for 3, and poor for 3. The randomized controlled trial showed noninferiority of an AI-DPP versus human coach–led DPP for the combined 12-month outcome (23/183, 12.6% vs 23/185, 12.4%; risk difference 0.1%, 1-sided 95% CI –5.5%). Program initiation (171/183, 93.4% vs 153/185, 82.7%; risk difference 10.7%, 95% CI 4.2%-17.3%) and completion (117/183, 63.9% vs 93/185, 50.3%; risk difference 13.7%; 95% CI 3.6%-23.7%) were higher with AI, but this did not translate into superior clinical outcomes. The nonrandomized comparison found no advantage of AI-personalized messaging over static messaging in terms of BMI or physical activity. The remaining studies reported uncontrolled changes precluding causal inference. Evidence was insufficient to determine whether effects differed by population or delivery setting. CONCLUSIONS One randomized trial supports noninferiority, not superiority, of a specific AI-driven DPP relative to human coaching; the remaining evidence was nonrandomized, predominantly commercially developed, and hypothesis-generating. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to stratify evidence on AI-driven diabetes prevention by AI mechanism—coaching, predictive, and conversational—and by outcome domain, extending prior scoping work that mapped apps without appraising study quality or comparative effectiveness. This structured mapping shows where evidence is the strongest (engagement and weight) and the weakest (glycemic causality and generalizability), giving health systems a concrete basis for deciding where AI-DPP tools may supplement, rather than replace, standard DPP delivery, pending independent, adequately powered randomized trials.

Customer experience (CX) is transformed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create value through AI advancement, with the collaboration of people for personalization and transparent interactions across the digital journey to gain a competitive advantage. This chapter creates premises that integrate and resolve contradictions in research on how CX creates value by using AI. Six literature fields were identified by a systematic review of articles that address how AI enables CX and value in the long term. To establish the research traditions by comparing the key concepts and metatheoretical assumptions addressed by each literature field, two concepts arise from analysis: customer experience and value emerge through AI advancement and adoption without human assistance, or it emerges through Human-AI collaboration. Identifying the alignment using a metatheoretical lens by research traditions forms four premises. These premises help to develop concepts about how experience creates value in the AI-driven world by explaining its framework and developing ideas for the future

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning technologies have significantly transformed financial markets and replaced intuition based strategies by data-driven intelligent systems. AI-driven trading and portfolio optimization platforms, which integrate advanced analytics, predictive modeling, and automated decision-making to enhance investment performance. The chapter explores the design and application of AI enabled trading platforms in modern financial markets. These platforms support technologies such as machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, natural language processing, and big data analytics to analyze market trends, detect trading opportunities, and construct optimized investment portfolios. By combining real-time and historical data, AI generate predictive insights for informed investment decisions and risk management strategies. The chapter discusses the evolution of algorithmic trading and AI's growing role in financial market analysis. It examines key components including data acquisition modules, predictive analytics engines, automated trading systems, and portfolio optimization models. Challenges such as model interpretability, regulatory compliance, data privacy, and algorithmic bias are also addressed. A conceptual framework is proposed for effective deployment of these technologies.

Generative AI is reshaping higher education's instructional video production, a domain once limited by cost, time, and specialized skills. This review examines how text-to-video synthesis, synthetic voice, automated editing, and AI-assisted authoring fit into the production lifecycle. Drawing on research from 2023–2026, it maps these tools against pre-production, production, and post-production stages, distinguishing between cognitive augmentation and output acceleration. Findings show AI-generated videos match traditional ones in learning outcomes while boosting efficiency, scalability, and multilingual access. However, risks include factual errors, loss of authenticity, and inequitable access. Contextualized within Philippine and ASEAN higher education, the chapter proposes a three-stage adoption framework (policy/governance, capability building, and equitable resourcing) to help educators adopt AI responsibly, concluding with policy implications.

Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource (HR) practices foster agile talent deployment within startup firms, particularly highlighting the mediating role of trust in AI and the moderating influence of digital culture climate. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on self-determination theory, the authors propose and empirically test a moderated mediation model using data collected from a three-wave, multisource survey of 298 employees working in three technology-oriented startups in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Structural equation modeling was used to examine the measurement and structural models and to test the hypothesized relationships among AI-enabled HR practices, trust in AI, digital culture climate and agile talent deployment. Findings Results reveal that AI-enabled HR practices positively influence agile talent deployment through increased employee trust in AI. In addition, the mediated relationship is stronger within organizations characterized by a robust digital culture climate, indicating that a digitally supportive organizational context enhances the effectiveness of AI-enabled HR initiatives. Originality/value The paper advances AI-enabled human resource management research by framing trust in AI as a mechanism translating supportive, transparent HR systems into agile talent deployment rather than technology acceptance. It identifies digital culture climate as an enactment condition enabling trust to become adaptive action. Practically, HR leaders should align explainable AI, trust-building practices and digital norms to strengthen workforce agility.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies can facilitate sport organizations’ forward-looking strategies, administration, accountability, and stakeholder communication. However, there is a need to consider leadership competencies, data utility, implementation infrastructure, and governance mechanisms. The purpose of this review article is to provide an Africa-centric analytical synthesis of AI-enabled leadership and digital governance in sport institutions. The review focuses on digital transformation, organizational dynamic capabilities, stakeholder governance, and responsible AI. Five conceptual areas were considered, including strategic leadership, data-driven decision-making, transparency and accountability, organizational readiness, and ethical and inclusive implementation. AI can enable financial audits, administrative reporting, resource allocation, performance evaluations, and stakeholder communications in sport organizations. However, there are risks associated with data privacy, algorithmic biases, cyber security, x- ai, digital divides, and reliance on external technologies. These factors could challenge the performance of sport organizations, particularly those with limited financial and infrastructural capabilities. The article provides a conceptual framework that connects institutional environments, AI-enabled leadership capabilities, digital governance mechanisms, and institutional transformation outcomes. Research gaps and implications were identified, including the need to study African sport-sponsoring entities, digital governance maturity models, financial accountability, and player data privacy. Since this is a review article, the proposed research strategy and thematic analysis need to go through a verifiable database search and screening process before the finalizing of the completed systematic review.

The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) demands innovative therapeutic strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly those originating from the human, animal, and environmental microbiome, represent a promising frontier within public health microbiology and microbial food safety. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have revolutionized the discovery pipeline, enabling high-throughput mining of metagenomic data and de novo generation of novel peptide sequences. This perspective review synthesizes recent breakthroughs in AI-driven discovery of microbiome-originated AMPs, examines their preclinical efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens under One Health and climate-sensitive frameworks and application in infectious disease treatment and discusses translational challenges including pharmacokinetics, toxicity, manufacturing scalability, and applications in food preservation and water safety. We argue that the convergence of microbiome science, deep learning, and synthetic biology positions AI-discovered AMPs as viable next-generation interventions against antibiotic resistance across human, animal, and environmental domains.

Radiological examinations increasingly leverage artificial intelligence to enhance diagnostic performance by compensating for expertise shortages, particularly in specialized interpretation. Despite academic AI models achieving compelling accuracy, adoption remains low. An objective, evidence-based examination of AI-guided clinical image interpretation seeks to expose the underlying reasons. The primary challenge lies not in accuracy but in fully automated analysis, especially for multimodal and multidimensional datasets. Introduction of uncertainty measures, image explainability, and real-world data reduce recognition to a decisive-supporting role— helping radiologists to detect previously unnoticed abnormalities—or even to precautionary analysis. Patients requesting precision medicine and therapy planning—and those at high risk of neglected pathology—stand to gain the greatest benefit. Relevant AI architecture considers imaging cues suitable for precision medicine or requiring additional methods to obtain interpretable images. Successful performance testing against an external, hidden reference dataset promotes vital user trust. Machine learning achieves best results where all potentially pathological abnormalities are identified and their presence virtually guaranteed, as in multi-class recognition. Data scarcity, however, impedes clinically relevant solutions. Explainability, essential for medical applications and clinical acceptance, extends simply beyond clinical decision support to provide saliency maps and, better still, clinically meaningful image regions or qualities. Attention maps may even bring a form of rule-based reasoning within reach. Clinical integration that reproduces the technical conditions under which model diagnostic measures are calculated raises the challenge of uncertainty quantification—a necessary condition for clinical decision support. Convolutional neural networks trained for photo-quality classification, par excellence supervised image quality assessment, provide the basic cues for uncertainty quantification. Imaging acquisition, modality, and systems are also defined in terms of current PACS/EPIC systems. PE, pre-symptomatic examination or precautionary examination, is defined as a patientuser group prepared to cover the cost of an examination with lower diagnostic accuracy and a high level of uncertainty

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Salivary-gland biopsy is central to Sjögren’s disease (SjD) assessment, but conventional measures incompletely capture glandular heterogeneity. This systematic review evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) applications to SjD salivary-gland histopathology and molecular profiling, including biological and translational validation. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched. Eligible studies used salivary-gland tissue as the primary analytical substrate or provided substantive glandular validation of systemic AI/ML findings. Evidence was synthesized functionally because of methodological heterogeneity. Results: Twenty-five studies were included. AI/ML identified histopathological and molecular phenotypes spanning immune/interferon activation, tissue architecture and immune-cell organization, epithelial stress and metabolic/cell-death remodeling, and translational response. Only a limited subset progressed beyond computational or tissue-level confirmation to functional perturbation, pharmacological testing, in vivo validation, or human treatment-response assessment. Recurrent public-dataset reuse, small cohorts, heterogeneous pipelines, and limited independent validation constrained reproducibility. Conclusions: AI/ML supports multidimensional SjD glandular phenotyping and shows emerging translational potential, but demonstrated clinical or therapeutic utility remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter validation is required before AI-derived glandular phenotypes can inform routine patient stratification or therapeutic decision-making.
topics: Salivary Gland Tumors Diagnosis and Treatment

documents.abstract: This study presents the Forest Fire Rescue Decision Support System (FFR-DSS), an AI-powered framework integrating GPT-4-based semantic analysis with real-time Twitter data to support emergency rescue coordination during forest fires in Turkey. Using tweets from the catastrophic 2021 wildfires affecting Muğla and Antalya, FFR-DSS employs prompt-engineered large language model (LLM) pipelines to extract urgency scores, emotional tone, geographical information, and actionability indicators from crisis-related social media content. Unlike traditional natural language processing (NLP) approaches such as Bag-of-Words (BoW) and TF-IDF, which may struggle with contextually rich and emotionally variable messages, the proposed framework leverages GPT-4's zero-shot semantic reasoning capabilities without requiring task-specific labeled training datasets. A geospatial risk mapping component further aggregates tweet-level outputs into district-level risk scores and dynamic heatmaps, enabling emergency teams to identify critical areas and prioritize resource allocation. Evaluation against a manually annotated sample demonstrates that FFR-DSS achieves 92.4% classification precision and 89.1% recall, substantially outperforming the BoW+SVM baseline with 72.8% accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of LLM-augmented social media analytics to transform unstructured crisis communications into actionable intelligence, improving situational awareness, rescue coordination, and data-driven decision-making during large-scale natural disasters.In addition to its natural language understanding capabilities, FFR-DSS incorporates a geospatial mapping component to visualize and monitor critical rescue zones dynamically. By aligning semantic outputs with location data, the system helps authorities prioritize interventions in areas of greatest need. Empirical evaluations show that FFR-DSS achieves higher classification accuracy and interpretability than prior baseline methods, offering a more robust, transparent, and context-aware framework for emergency response. The results suggest that GPT-based systems represent a transformative step in disaster management technology, particularly in scenarios requiring rapid analysis and decision-making based on unstructured social media content.

Background and Objective: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) present major challenges in clinical care, impacting patient safety and therapeutic outcomes. Traditional detection methods, often based on curated databases, may miss newly emerging interactions or require frequent manual updates. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI) offer novel tools for real-time, automated DDI detection directly from biomedical literature. This study introduces an AI-powered approach to identify DDIs, assign relevance scores to publications, and benchmark performance against conventional databases. Methods: We developed an NLP pipeline incorporating sentence classification to detect safety and interaction-related content, and named entity recognition (NER) to extract drug-drug interaction types, their clinical impact, and patient features. The sentence classification module is based on a BERT architecture fine-tuned from microsoft/BiomedNLP-BiomedBERT-baseuncased-abstract-fulltext, and the NER module uses the open-source model d4data/biomedical-ner-all. A DDI relevance score was designed to quantify each article’s significance based on weighted parameters derived from model outputs, with weights informed by domain experts (title relevance: 50 points, DDI impact: 40 points, publication type: 10 points). The system was validated on a manually curated dataset. We applied ANOVA and sensitivity analyses, and evaluated performance using recall, precision, and F1-score, comparing our method to established DDI resources. Key Content and Findings: The pipeline was validated on 7,751 articles across 15 query types. ROC analysis identified a relevance score threshold of 75%. Drug-family queries achieved the highest F1-score (0.872), followed by single-drug (0.731) and drug-drug queries (0.684). ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc analysis confirmed statistically significant differences in relevance scores between annotation groups (p < 0.05), with full stratification across all three groups for drug-drug family queries. Compared with manually compiled expert reference lists, our system retrieved substantially more relevant articles without requiring manual updates. Conclusion: AI-driven NLP approaches can enhance clinical decision support systems by providing comprehensive, evidence-based DDI detection and prioritization, offering scalable support for safer pharmacological decision-making. Keywords: Drug-drug Interactions; Natural Language Processing; Artificial Intelligence; Pharmacovigilance; Clinical Decision Support.

Abstract By enabling sentiment analysis, targeted advertising, automated moderation, tailored content recommendations, and generative content production, artificial intelligence (AI) has radically changed social media platforms. AI-powered social media has improved civic engagement, political communication, and public awareness, strengthening democratic participation. However, it has also brought about serious problems, such as deep fakes, algorithmic bias, political polarization, electoral manipulation, misinformation, and privacy threats. These trends have significant ramifications for electoral integrity, public trust, and democratic governance. This study looks at the advantages and disadvantages of AI-powered social media for democracy and makes policy suggestions for maintaining moral AI governance while defending democratic principles.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in the advertising industry, enabling brands to produce video content that is personalized, visually engaging, scalable, and cost‑effective. Despite these advantages, the proliferation of AI in advertising raises significant ethical concerns, particularly regarding authenticity, transparency, privacy, misinformation, and deepfakes. These issues are especially relevant among college students, who encounter advertisements extensively through social media platforms. This study investigates the perceptions of AI‑generated video advertisements among college students in Mumbai, with a focus on ethics, authenticity, and trust. A quantitative research design was employed, and primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms. The final sample consisted of 91 respondents, who provided insights into their social media usage, perceptions of AI‑driven advertising, and concerns related to ethical practices. The findings indicate that lack of transparency was the most prominent ethical concern (42%), followed by privacy misuse (30%) and misleading content or deepfakes (20%). Respondents emphasized the importance of clear disclosure of AI involvement, truthful communication, human oversight, protection of personal data, and avoidance of misleading or stereotypical representations. The study concludes that students do not categorically reject AI‑generated advertising; rather, their acceptance is contingent upon responsible and transparent application of AI technologies. Overall, the results highlight that technological innovation in advertising must be supported by authenticity, ethical communication, transparency, and human oversight to strengthen trust among college students in Mumbai. These insights contribute to ongoing debates on digital ethics and the responsible integration of AI in advertising practices. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI-Generated Video Advertisements, College Students, Advertising Ethics, Social Media
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This perspective paper reviews recent advancements and explores future, exciting opportunities for both artificial intelligence (AI)‐powered smart displays and AI‐assisted augmented reality (AR) eyeglasses. To begin, we analyze fundamental AI‐enhanced image‐quality techniques, including perceptual resolution upscaling algorithms, tone mapping, reverse tone mapping, and image‐quality analysis. Next, we examine the practical implementations of AI technologies for smart displays, in which both the visual experience and use case of novel display technologies can be improved. Finally, we further explore AI integration into wearable AR glasses, highlighting the enabled capabilities to improve display systems through waveguide combiner optimization and image correction, and exploring recent advances that go beyond color in AR glasses, such as eye tracking, foveated rendering, and physiological sensing. By outlining emerging trends and promising directions for next‐generation display technologies, this perspective will demonstrate the critical role of AI in enabling new capabilities, user experiences, and technological breakthroughs in the field of displays.

Urban air pollution is one of the most persistent environmental and public-health problems facing Indian cities, and Delhi in particular records some of the highest particulate matter concentrations in the world during the post-monsoon and winter months. Public air-quality portals in India largely display current or historical readings, but they rarely tell a city administrator what the air will look like over the next few days, or where a pollution spike is likely originating from. This gap between “knowing today's AQI” and “deciding what to do about it” motivates AirSense AI, a full-stack urban air-quality intelligence platform designed as an academic prototype for Delhi. The system ingests PM2.5, PM10 and NO₂ station readings together with weather variables, satellite fire detections and land-use information, converts pollutant concentrations into a standardized Air Quality Index using the U.S. EPA methodology, and applies a gradient-boosted decision tree model (XGBoost) to forecast AQI up to 72 hours ahead. In parallel, the platform combines NASA FIRMS active-fire data with OpenStreetMap land-use polygons and Haversine-distance calculations to rank probable pollution hotspots, and uses a large language model (Groq/LLaMA 3) to translate the resulting numerical evidence into readable, bilingual (English/Hindi) advisories and enforcement summaries for administrators and citizens. The results are presented through a React and Leaflet-based interactive dashboard. This paper describes the motivation, related work, and proposed architecture of AirSense AI as an integrated decision-support system rather than a monitoring-only tool. As the platform is at the prototype stage, no experimental forecasting accuracy, source-attribution validation, or user-study results are reported here; these are identified as required additions for the next version of this paper.

This study examines how algorithmic management in the gig economy is related to gig workers' workplace wellbeing. Specifically, we explore how algorithmic management corresponds with (positive) challenge appraisal and (negative) threat appraisal. We also examine the moderating role of psychological resilience in these relationships, as well as the implications of appraisal processes for workplace wellbeing. Data were collected from 389 food delivery workers in China. We find that algorithmic management is positively associated with both challenge appraisal and threat appraisal. Challenge appraisal is positively associated with workplace wellbeing, whereas threat appraisal is negatively associated with workplace wellbeing. Psychological resilience strengthens the challenge-appraisal pathway and the corresponding positive indirect relationship with workplace wellbeing, but it does not significantly buffer the threat-appraisal pathway. These findings show that algorithmic management is associated with both positive and negative appraisal processes and that psychological resilience may play different roles across these pathways. The study therefore offers a more nuanced explanation of the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing.

Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for reliable, efficient, and interpretable machine learning (ML) methods for complex prediction and decision-making tasks. However, conventional ML approaches often encounter challenges related to model optimization, generalization, computational efficiency, data imbalance, and limited interpretability. This study proposes an Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction that integrates data preprocessing, feature engineering, algorithm selection, Hyperparameter optimization, ensemble learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Multiple ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gradient Boosting, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, are comparatively evaluated. Model performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), computational efficiency, and interpretability. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME techniques are incorporated to explain feature contributions and improve transparency in model predictions. The framework facilitates systematic comparison between conventional and optimized models while examining the trade-off between predictive performance, computational cost, and explainability. The proposed approach provides a generalizable pathway for developing robust and trustworthy intelligent prediction systems. Its applicability extends across healthcare, education, cyber security, finance, and other data-driven domains. The study contributes an integrated framework that combines algorithmic optimization with explainability to support accurate, transparent, efficient, and reliable ML-based decision-making systems.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Phenotyping is fundamental to rare disease diagnosis, but manually curating structured phenotypes from clinical notes is labor intensive and difficult to scale. Existing artificial intelligence (AI) approaches optimize individual components of phenotyping but generally do not operationalize the full workflow of extracting features from clinical text, standardizing them to Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, and prioritizing rare disease-relevant HPO terms. We developed RARE-PHENIX, an end-to-end AI framework for rare disease phenotyping that integrates large language model-based phenotype extraction, ontology-grounded standardization to HPO terms, and supervised ranking of HPO terms. We trained RARE-PHENIX using data from 2671 patients across 11 Undiagnosed Diseases Network clinical sites, and externally validated it on 16,357 real-world clinical notes from 143 patients at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Our findings suggest RARE-PHENIX generates structured, prioritized HPO terms highly concordant with clinician curation, demonstrates potential downstream disease-prioritization signal, and may support human-in-the-loop rare disease phenotyping in real-world settings.

documents.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have had a substantial impact on software engineering research and practice, as well as on software engineering education. In Software Engineering (SE) education, prior studies have mainly examined students’ LLM usage through surveys, interviews, or short-term observations, offering limited visibility into their actual development activities. As a result, it remains unclear how students’ perceptions of LLM usage match their actual development practices. To address this gap, we analyze course project data collected over three years from 158 students enrolled in an upper-level SE course, together with students’ experience-sharing presentations, survey responses, and activity logs. We examine LLM integration by jointly analyzing students’ perceived usage and usefulness from surveys and presentations, their actual development activities captured through VS Code activity logs, and their project performance based on evaluation results across different levels of LLM support. By combining these analyses, we connect students’ reported LLM usage with their actual development activities and assess its relation to learning outcomes in SE course projects. Our results show that students utilized LLMs frequently for code-related tasks and generally found them helpful, with frequent usage increasing over the course project while perceptions shifted as project complexity grew. Activity log analysis revealed divergent patterns in LLM usage, reflecting both increasing dependency and deliberate efforts to maintain development independence. Across three years, integrating LLM support did not lead to statistically significant differences in final project achievement as measured by requirement satisfaction, although students with LLM support produced substantially larger software systems and lower-performing teams showed mild benefits, suggesting that LLMs may help reduce the influence of programming proficiency on project outcomes. Our findings highlight both the benefits and tensions of LLM integration in SE course projects and suggest that future SE course designs may incorporate more complex and challenging SE tasks beyond implementation-focused requirements, while also providing explicit education on prompt engineering, supporting students’ code comprehension of rapidly generated LLM-assisted code, and helping students avoid excessive dependency on LLM tools during development.
